The tree design borrows from the B+ tree only bulk loading at a fill factor and a node capacity for what must share one window; fill_factor 0.75 sits in thresholds.json marked 'design R47, later', no script under research-tree reads it, and tcb/plan-tree.mjs does not exist.

A tree leaf has two capacities: pack capacity C_node, computed in commit.mjs as W_quality minus the child prefix minus the review reserve (300000, 60000 and 75000 tokens in thresholds.json, all three marked guess), and spend A_leaf with soft and hard fractions 0.8 and 0.9 of the task estimate.

The coordinator's hand-over window follows the square-root law W* = P + S + √(2H0·g); W_star_coord = 133200 tokens in thresholds.json is computed by cost.mjs from estimated or guessed inputs, not measured on a tree run.

claim: The decision rule says units that last minutes with 3 to 16 workers are not covered by its papers; it acts only at the gate, stops running work only for memory at its floor, and puts ordered sequences under one owner at a time.

The second protocol's budget cut stops running work (at the watcher's urgent exit the coordinator stops the child, the task cut, its uncovered ids kept), while the decision rule stops running work only for memory at its floor; the two documents disagree on budget as a reason to stop, and the overflow that would trigger a split comes from that cut.

claim: cost.mjs sizes the root's fan-out as the status rows of about 200 tokens (a guess) that fit in the whole room between P + S and the coordinator's W*, and prints from it that no inner level is needed; by the hand-over law that room, √(2H0·g) = g·k*, is the coordinator's own window growth over one epoch, so child summaries share it with its own calls.
note: Found by the refuter on claim C83; s_summary and the share of g are not measured.

claim: The tree lane (t1) of research round 3 folded its claims as 65 confirmed, 42 holding in part, 5 refuted and 3 that cannot be checked; refuted and not to be proposed again: C51, merging child summaries once at the top as in lazy leveling (every parent call re-reads its window, so reads dominate, where leveling is best); C59, a minimum work per session from Gray and Graefe's page law (it is the optimum of a log utility, not an overhead floor, and neither premise holds for sessions); C90, that the B-link form settles the record's split conflict (it gives a split's mechanism, not the choice between split and hand-over, so the conflict stays open); C108, that PostgreSQL finishes a split later by a named job (it posts the downlink at once, and only after a failure does the next writer finish it); C114, that FoundationDB's 5-second window means a unit that outgrows its window is split (it is a reason to keep units short; the record's rule there is a hand-over).

Lehman and Yao: when a node splits it is replaced by two, the first one's link pointer reaching the second; the link must exist before the parent's pointer, so a node with a left twin and no parent is a legal state, and the link serves as a temporary fix that allows correct concurrent operation.
Lehman and Yao: a search does no locking of any kind, and an insert locks at most three nodes at once, relatively infrequently, only when following a link while inserting a pointer to a split node.

Lehman and Yao do not merge: deletion allows fewer than K entries in a leaf, and low occupancy is left to a batch reorganisation or an underflow operation that locks the entire tree, under the assumption that insertions take place more often than deletions.

Lehman and Yao measured nothing (the system's behaviour 'could be quantified by simulation'), and their scheme does not prevent livelock of a process on a relatively very slow processor that keeps following links, an argument made for processors of comparable speeds.

Graefe's survey of B-tree locking: a B-link split is a local step affecting only one existing node; posting to the parent can be a side effect of any later root-to-leaf traversal, should happen as soon as possible, and may be delayed past a reboot or a crash without data loss or inconsistency; high insertion rates risk long linked lists of neighbours.
Bw-tree (Levandoski, Lomet and Sengupta): a thread that sees a partial structure change completes it before its own operation, posting the split's index term delta to the parent first (help-along).

Bw-tree paper, Table I (latch-free delta update failures): failed splits 0.25% dedup, 1.27% Xbox, 8.88% synthetic; failed consolidates 1.19% dedup, 0.22% Xbox, 7.35% synthetic; the text beside it gives one rounded figure for Xbox and dedup that matches neither dedup splits nor Xbox consolidates.
Bw-tree paper, the designers' own benchmark in memory: 10.4M operations/second against BerkeleyDB's 555K on the Xbox workload, a speedup of 18.7x.

Wang and others (OpenBw-Tree rebuild): the Bw-tree's indirection layer and delta records make it under-perform the lock-based indexes (a B+ tree and ART with optimistic lock coupling, Masstree) by 1.5-4.5x; being lock-free, its threads are not guaranteed progress because of failed CaS, and help-along is how it eases that starvation.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C27): the draft gave help-along the defect it is meant to ease.

claim: Leis and others (optimistic lock coupling, B-tree of 100M values on a 10-core system): with 20 threads OLC looks up 3.9x faster than traditional lock coupling; single-threaded, all three approaches perform very similarly.

Leis and others: the B-link tree holds a single lock at a time, and releasing the parent lock early is highly beneficial when the child node must be fetched from disk; the comparison assumes no merge operations are implemented.

ARIES/IM (Mohan and Levine): structure changes in one index tree are serialised by a tree latch taken in X mode just before the change at the leaf and held until all its effects reach up the tree; its holder does no I/O under it, so the hold should be very small (no figure); concurrent structure changes need a lock and risk deadlock.
ARIES/IM: a structure change is performed as a nested top action, so a transaction that rolls back after completing it bypasses the change's log records and does not undo it.

Srinivasan and Carey (simulation, curves not read as numbers): B-link algorithms gave the most concurrency and the best overall performance; with one CPU and one disk the algorithms barely differ, except under very high contention among appends with the tree in memory, where a pessimistic algorithm won because link-chases grew enormously; real systems usually merge pages only when they become empty.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C34): the draft said the algorithms barely differ with one CPU and one disk without the contention exception.

claim: Arge's buffer tree: an update is put in the root's buffer and pushed one level down only when a buffer runs full, for an amortised O(log_m n / B) I/Os per operation; the structure serves batched (off-line) problems whose answers need not be immediate.
Arge's buffer tree empties a node's buffer before every rebalance operation touches the node, so no structure change meets half-delivered messages.

Bender and others (B-epsilon trees): batching messages divides the insertion cost by the batch size B^(1−ε); with B = 1024 and ε = 1/2 inserts run 16 times faster, while point queries cost a constant factor 1/ε more, at most twice as many I/Os at ε = 1/2.
B-epsilon trees flush messages to a child only when a node's buffer is full, and only to children with enough pending messages to offset the cost of rewriting the parent.
In a B-epsilon tree a query must check the buffers of the nodes on its root-to-leaf path and apply the relevant messages before returning its result.

BetrFS worked model (1TB of 1KB records, a B-epsilon tree of 1MB nodes and fan-out 10, all but the leaves in memory): height about 7, each item takes part in 14 I/Os, a flush moves 100 items, so 14/100 I/Os per item against 2 in a B-tree, 14.3 times faster inserts; the gain is items per flush over the depth and grows as items shrink.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C42): the draft said items per flush over twice the depth.

claim: Luo and Carey's LSM survey: leveling merges more often and costs T times more in writes than tiering; tiering is optimised for writes at the cost of query performance and space, though point lookups lose little thanks to Bloom filters while range queries and space suffer; many reported gains were measured against untuned LevelDB or RocksDB.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C45): the draft said tiering costs T times in reads without the Bloom filter condition.

claim: Dostoevsky (Dayan and Idreos): Lazy Leveling removes merging from all levels but the largest, improving the worst-case update cost while keeping the bounds on point lookups, long range lookups and space and giving only a competitive bound on short range lookups; no single merge policy rules: as the proportion of lookups grows, the best fixed policy moves from tiering through Lazy Leveling to leveling.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C46): the draft gave the same bounds on all lookups.

claim: Rosenblum and Ousterhout (log-structured file system): the segments cleaned must have a utilization of less than .8 for a log-structured file system to outperform the current Unix FFS, and less than .5 to outperform an improved FFS.

Rodeh (copy-on-write B-trees, IBM report): under shadowing a change rewrites its path, and in the worst case, when a node is split or fixed on the way down, the modified disk pages can be 2 x tree-depth.
Rodeh: trees built by an append-only workload had an average occupancy of 50%, because the right edge of the tree keeps splitting and leaves half-full nodes behind.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C53): this holds for Rodeh's top-down tree with middle splits; engines that split at the arrival point keep sequential pages near full (t1-0348, t1-0350).

claim: Rodeh: in his copy-on-write B-tree every modification locks the root and one of its children exclusively, a serialisation point that was not a problem in practice because the root and its children were almost always cached.

Becker and others (multiversion B-tree): a version split copies only the live entries into a fresh block, with slack such that at least ε·d + 1 inserts or deletes pass before that block's next structure change.

Gray and Graefe (page size by a ratio): index page utility is the binary log of entries per page and access cost is disk latency plus page size over transfer rate; in their table 16 KB pages score best, 0.78; index height is about the binary log of N over the binary log of entries per page.

LMDB documentation: data pages are copy-on-write, writes are fully serialised (one write transaction at a time), writers never block readers nor readers writers, and long-lived read transactions prevent reuse of pages freed by newer writes.

Comer's survey: B*-tree insertion redistributes locally and delays splitting until 2 sibling nodes are full, then divides the 2 nodes into 3 each 2/3 full, guaranteeing storage utilisation of at least 66% instead of 1/2 for a plain B-tree.

Kim and others (agent architecture scaling study, coordination table): trace-level error amplification is 17.2 for independent agents against 4.4 for a centralised system (one orchestrator over three agents) and 1.0 for one agent; success per 1K tokens is 67.7 for one agent against 21.5 centralised; after controlling for other coordination metrics error amplification is not a significant predictor.

Kim and others: coordination turns grow as a power law in agent count, 2.72 × (n + 0.5)^1.724 with fit 0.974, and at a matched budget of about 4,800 reasoning tokens per trial per-agent reasoning becomes prohibitively thin beyond 3-4 agents.

Huang and others (resilience to one faulty agent): the hierarchical structures drop -5.51 against -10.54 for flat and -23.72 for linear ones, where hierarchical means MAD (two debaters and one judge) and AgentVerse (four agents): depth one, different systems, not a test of depth.

Dremel, 2900 leaf servers held constant (Figure 11, times not read): with 2 levels Q3, an aggregation returning many groups, was off the chart because the root aggregated near-sequentially; 3 levels (1:100:2900) ran it and a fourth (1:10:100:2900) halved Q3 again, while Q2 ran in 3 seconds at three levels and gained little.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C70): the draft said the extra level halved another query; it halved Q3, the many-group aggregation.

claim: Astrolabe (van Renesse and others, simulation): at 390,625 members and branching factor 5 the zone tree has 8 levels and each member keeps and gossips only 8 × 5 = 40 summaries.

TAG (Madden and others, sensor networks): in-network aggregation can reduce communication by an order of magnitude against sending everything to the root and at worst (MEDIAN) equals it; in a flat single-hop network it is no better than the centralised approach.

MacNet (agent topologies): average scores chain 0.6078, star 0.6267, tree 0.6015, with no confidence intervals in the text; at equal density wider star-shaped topologies generally beat deeper tree-shaped ones, which the paper ties to its own solution propagation.

Anthropic's multi-agent research system (self-reported, a company's account of its own production system with no method or public baseline): in its data multi-agent systems used about 15× more tokens than chats; subagents store work externally and pass lightweight references to the lead, and near the context limit an agent spawns fresh subagents with careful handoffs.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C74): marked self-reported.

claim: Erlang/OTP supervisors: if more than MaxR restarts occur within the last MaxT seconds the supervisor terminates its children and then itself, and the next higher supervisor decides; intensity and period default to 1 and 5.

RAO (trained recursive agents), TextCraft-Synth tasks both methods solved: the recursive agent used 196K tokens against the single agent's 1029K, of which 1021K were cache reads; single-agent tokens grow quadratically with steps because each step re-encodes the history, much of which KV caching eases.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claims C76, C81): the saving is mostly cache reads, so it shows in token count more than in token cost.

claim: RAO: on DeepDive, whose sub-tasks depend on each other in sequence, the recursive agent was 18x slower on tasks both solved, though with a much higher success rate; 83.9% of TextCraft-Synth's subagent calls ran concurrently against 1.6% of DeepDive's delegations.

RAO: the recursive agent was 1.8x and 2.5x faster on medium and hard TextCraft-Synth tasks; on Oolong-Real the single agent was 14x faster, but trained at 32K context and unable to print the 55K+ input it used fast inaccurate heuristics such as regex, while the recursive agent read the context in chunks through subagents with much higher accuracy.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C76): Oolong's token cost buys a different, more accurate strategy, not the re-read case.

claim: Self-organising LLM teams (simulated tasks): scaling from 4 to 64 agents, the self-formed hierarchy depth rose from 1.0 to only 2.0, at most two management layers without external design.

ReDel (recursive delegation by prompted models): two failure modes, overcommitment (an agent attempts an overly complex task itself) and undercommitment (an agent does no work and re-delegates its task), with delegation stopped by a configured depth limit or a timeout.

PostgreSQL's B-tree is a Lehman and Yao tree: it adds a right-link to each page's right sibling and a high key, so pages are searched without holding read locks except to keep the one page being read from changing.

PostgreSQL: since 9.4 an interrupted B-tree split or page deletion is finished lazily at the next insertion or vacuum rather than at the end of recovery, which made recovery much more complicated; a split flags the left page INCOMPLETE_SPLIT and keeps it locked until the parent has its downlink, so the flag is seen only after a failed insertion into the parent, and then the next writer that meets it finishes the split.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C95): the draft said splits are finished lazily as the rule; normally the split is finished at once.

claim: PostgreSQL deletes a B-tree page only when it is completely empty and never merges partly full pages, since moving items left or right seems impractical with concurrent scans; it never deletes the rightmost page of a level, so the tree's height cannot decrease.

PostgreSQL splits the root the same way as any other page and then constructs a new root holding pointers to both halves; searches that read the old root pointer still find data moved to the right sibling through the right-link.
InnoDB manual: InnoDB leaves 1/16 of a page free; index records inserted in sequential order give pages about 15/16 full, in random order from 1/2 to 15/16 full.
InnoDB manual: when an index page's fill drops below MERGE_THRESHOLD, 50% by default, InnoDB tries to contract the index tree to free the page.

LMDB source (mdb.c): with MDB_APPEND a page splits at the new key, leaving the old page full; otherwise the split is in the middle, biased so the new page is emptier than the old when the new item goes on the page's last spot, for better packing during sequential inserts.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C99): the draft left out the bias for sequential inserts.

claim: LMDB source: FILL_THRESHOLD is 250, the minimum page fill in tenths of a percent; pages emptier than this are candidates for merging.
RocksDB at Facebook (CIDR paper, self-reported): under read/write workloads like Facebook's, B-tree pages are only 1/2 to 2/3 full, as measured in Facebook production databases.

RocksDB at Facebook (review of MySQL installations, self-reported): RocksDB used about 50% less storage than InnoDB with compression, wrote between 10% and 15% of what InnoDB wrote, and did 10% - 20% more reads.

MyRocks at Facebook (self-reported, one workload): approximately 25% to 30% of each InnoDB block was wasted by index fragmentation, and B-tree defragmentation was less effective than expected because a continuous stream of mostly random writes quickly fragmented pages just defragmented.

RocksDB team (self-reported): leveled write amplification in the 10-30 range was too high for write-heavy applications, so they added tiered compaction, which brings it down to the 4-10 range at lower read performance.

RocksDB team (self-reported): of 42 surveyed production deployments of ZippyDB and MyRocks most were space constrained, and space efficiency is the bottleneck for most applications using SSDs; what binds changed over the years.

FoundationDB (self-reported): a 5-second MVCC window limits the memory of resolvers and storage servers and so restricts transaction sizes; it is long enough for the majority of OLTP use cases, and of transactions that would span more than 5s many can be divided into smaller transactions.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C103): the draft said long work can usually be divided; the source says many.

claim: Discord (company blog, self-reported, uncontrolled): after the move from Cassandra to ScyllaDB, fetching historical messages went from a p99 of between 40-125ms to 15ms, with the store and the front data service changed together.

Discord (self-reported): a hot partition frequently affected latency across the whole database cluster; request coalescing (one database query for many identical requests) and hash-based routing to the data services helped a lot but did not end hot partitions.
Uber (company blog, self-reported): in Postgres the primary and secondary indexes point directly to on-disk tuple offsets, so when a tuple location changes all indexes must be updated.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C105): Uber's further statement that B-tree rebalancing moves sub-trees is its own and does not match PostgreSQL's B-tree (t1-0346).

claim: Pebble (design note, no measurement): flushes are paced by keeping the bytes still to be flushed from the memtables at a constant level, compactions by keeping an estimate of compaction debt at a target, slowed below it, so both run only as fast as needed and latency spikes for user reads and writes fall.
note: Narrowed by the refuter (claim C106): the draft said both were paced by compaction debt.

claim: Untested: for a small job known up front (leaves the packer makes, L, at most b, the children one parent holds per epoch; realised over estimated work per leaf, R, rarely above 1/f; no new keys during the run), the bulk-loaded two-level tree we have fits, with f computed from R, and nothing splits, merges or latches while work runs.

Untested: for a job that grows (new keys during a run, or R above 1/f at some leaves), add a split in the B-link form for unstarted keys only: the new leaf first, linked by the overflow record, its index posted after by one script step under the run lock; a separator only where keys are worked in key order, otherwise a list of ids; a small remainder goes to an unstarted sibling or the next wave, since a new leaf pays a full start; no merge.

Untested: for a very large project (L greater than b), price more coordinator epochs against an inner level and take the one that costs fewer tokens; add a level only where its summary is much smaller than its inputs and its children run at once; where levels win, depth is the ceiling of log_b L, width before depth.

Untested (rank 1 by the size of the cost it acts on, not by a measured gain): fewer parent wakes in the research tree; a wake waits while nothing in the backlog is urgent, the backlog is counted in tokens, and the trigger weighs the fixed re-read of the parent's window against the cost of delay, since a held-back correction lets a running leaf spend on stale work.

Untested (rank 2): pack the tree's leaves at plan time with f = 1/q_{1−p}(R), R the leaf's realised over estimated work, one f per capacity, so a leaf overflows with chance p; fewer, fuller leaves, since an under-full leaf still costs its admission and end wakes, a slot and a memory peak.

Untested (rank 3): split unstarted keys in the B-link form, posted by one script step under the run lock, with a small remainder sent to an unstarted sibling or the next wave and no merge; it never fires for a small job, fires once per overflow for a growing one, and stays local to one leaf zone for a very large one.

Untested (rank 4): when one coordinator cannot hold its children per epoch, choose between more coordinator epochs and an inner level by tokens; depth is the ceiling of log_b L where levels win, width first, and levels go only where they compress and their children run concurrently.

Untested (rank 5, replaces the refuted 'merge once at the top'): each inner node of a very large tree keeps one bounded summary per child, rewritten per report, because every parent call re-reads its window, so reads dominate, the end of Dostoevsky's curve where leveling is best.

Untested (rank 6, mostly exists): copy-on-write records with one writer per shared file (tree-plan.json and the task table through a script under the run lock), readers on snapshots, keys named by question id and found through one map, so a split rewrites one map entry.
Untested (rank 7, only when observed): drop duplicate messages in the parent's buffer for a leaf woken by many messages, and bound restarts per parent before escalating.

Measure, from coordinator transcripts on disk (no run needed), a parent's tokens per wake split into the fixed re-read of its window and what each child adds (s_summary), and how many wakes could have waited; it sets b, the gain of fewer wakes and where the small case of the research tree ends.
Measure R, the realised over estimated work of each leaf, from the pilot's predicted-against-realised log (R48(a)), per class of question; it sets f per capacity and how often leaves overflow.

Measure a tree session's start cost (child prefix P and reloaded state S0, now 60,000 and 10,000 tokens by guess) and its time on a tree run; against the unstarted remainder at an overflow it decides between a new leaf, an unstarted sibling and the next wave.

Measure on the pilot and later runs the new keys per leaf lifetime and whether a field works its keys in key order (the start order of keys in the ledger); they decide whether a split is needed and whether it can route by a separator or must move a list of ids.

Measure, before any inner level is added to the research tree, how much an inner session compresses (tokens out over tokens read) and the share of its children that run at once; a level pays only where both are high, which no session study has measured.
Measure a parent's read share (how often it reads state against how often children report); it sets the merge policy of inner summaries.
Count repeated or overlapping questions per leaf and session restarts per hour once tree runs exist; they decide whether a dedupe step and a restart bound per parent are needed.

proposed correction of x03-0335: Bw-tree Table I gives failed splits 0.25% dedup, 1.27% Xbox, 8.88% synthetic and failed consolidates 1.19%, 0.22%, 7.35%; the about 1.25% on Xbox and dedup is the text's rounded figure and matches neither dedup splits nor Xbox consolidates.

proposed correction of x21-0318: 4.4 against 17.2 is trace-level error amplification of a centralised system (one orchestrator over three agents) against three independent agents, and after controls error amplification is not a significant predictor; -5.51 against -23.72 compares different systems of depth one (a judge over two debaters; AgentVerse's four agents) with linear ones, not a test of depth.

proposed correction of x21-0470: the 246 rows of about 200 tokens fill the whole room between P plus S and W*, which by the hand-over law is g·k*, the coordinator's own window growth over one epoch; rows of child summaries share that room with its own calls, so the bound counts it twice, and a bound for sessions needs s_summary and the share of g, neither measured.
note: The 7-10 fields that record covers stay far below the bound either way; the correction is to the reason, not the conclusion.

claim: Measure a research child's reloaded state S and its growth per epoch on a run under option (b), against g·k*; R49's ratio then decides between handing over and splitting when a field outgrows its window, the conflict the record leaves open.
